title: Mounting fabric in a wooden hoop
subtitle: Getting the cloth drum-tight for smooth counting and clean stitches.
excerpt: A wooden hoop holds the cloth under even tension so stitches go in straight and even. The inner ring goes under the cloth, the outer ring locks over it, and the screw is tightened while the cloth is smoothed taut.
sourceNotes:

aliases: how to use an embroidery hoop

glossaryTerms.definition: The solid inner circle of a two-piece embroidery hoop. The fabric lies over this ring; the outer ring then locks down on top. The inner ring has no screw.

The even tautness of cloth held in an embroidery hoop. Correct tension allows the needle to pass through without distorting the weave, and keeps completed stitches from puckering when the hoop is removed.

content.text: Mounting fabric in a wooden hoop is the first practical step in any counted embroidery or surface embroidery project. The
hoop tension
keeps the weave square and makes counting accurate. Poor tension creates puckered stitches that don't press out.
What you need

items.name: Fabric, pre-cut with at least 5 cm border around the design area

content.text: How to mount the fabric
Loosen the screw on the outer ring so the two rings separate easily.
Place the
inner ring
on a flat surface and lay the fabric centred over it, design area centred.
Press the outer ring down over the inner ring and fabric. The screw notch goes at the top.
Tighten the screw finger-tight only. Do not fully tighten yet.
Hold the hoop in one hand and use the other to smooth the fabric taut from the edges toward the screw. Pull north, south, east, and west in turn, keeping the grain square.
Once the fabric is drum-taut and the grain is square, tighten the screw fully. The fabric should not shift or pucker when you lightly flick the surface.
Protecting the fabric from hoop marks

On fine evenweave and linen, the inner hoop ring can leave a permanent ring mark. To prevent this, wrap the inner ring with a thin strip of washed cotton tape before mounting. The tape provides a softer grip and reduces slipping too.
Common mistakes

attrs.heading: What goes wrong
attrs.intro: Four mounting problems and how to correct them.

items.symptom: The fabric puckers in the hoop
items.cause: The screw was tightened before the fabric was smoothed taut, trapping puckers in the cloth.
items.fix: Loosen the screw, smooth the fabric taut in all four directions, then re-tighten.

items.symptom: The grain is skewed in the hoop
items.cause: The fabric was placed over the inner ring at an angle.
items.fix: Remove, straighten the grain by eye or against a ruled mat, and remount.

items.symptom: The fabric slips in the hoop during stitching
items.cause: Worn or polished inner ring, or the screw is too loose.
items.fix: Wrap the inner ring with cotton tape. Tighten the screw more firmly.

items.symptom: A ring mark appears on the cloth after removing
items.cause: The hoop was left mounted in one position for an extended period.
items.fix: Remove the fabric from the hoop at the end of every session. Wash out any mark with cool water before it sets.

content.text: What this underpins
Correct hoop mounting is the foundation of every embroidery discipline.
Mounting fabric in a hoop
also underpins the Q-snap and scroll-frame mounting methods, which follow the same tension-first principle.
